BOI.name: Boise
BOI.excerpt: Friday, a closed low off the Pacific Northwest Coast amplifies along a southward trough axis capturing a pocket of tropical moisture. As a deep Alaskan Low strengthens, it captures the closed low, trough, and tropical moisture.

sections.name: Key Messages
paragraphs: - Isolated to scattered showers today, greatest coverage northern mountain zones with minor snow accumulations above 6000 ft MSL.
- Gradual clearing this evening with temperatures around 5 degrees below normal through Wednesday.
- Dry and warmer Thursday, precipitation chances increasing Friday into the weekend.

sections.name: Short Term
paragraphs: A weak shortwave disturbance will track across the region this afternoon and evening, generating isolated showers mainly over higher terrain and northern mountain zones. Precipitation amounts will remain light. Any lingering shower activity will diminish rapidly late this evening with the departure of the shortwave.

Skies will clear tonight behind the exiting disturbance, promoting efficient radiational cooling. Low temperatures Wednesday morning will dip into the lower to mid 30s across many lower valleys, with freezing temperatures expected in higher valleys. This will support patchy frost development Wednesday morning.

A weak upper level ridge will build overhead Wednesday into Thursday ahead of a deepening low pressure system off the Pacific Northwest coast. This pattern will bring dry conditions and a slight warming trend, with daytime high temperatures rebounding closer to seasonal normals. Another round of patchy to widespread frost is possible early Thursday morning across valley locations, as mostly clear skies and light winds foster even better radiational cooling conditions than the previous night.

By late Thursday and Thursday night, the offshore low will dig further south off the Pacific Northwest coast, shifting flow aloft to a more southerly to southwesterly direction. This will begin to advect mid and upper level moisture northeastward from the southwestern United States into the northern Great Basin. Ensemble guidance suggest sufficient moisture and weak lift could trigger isolated to scattered light showers across the central Idaho mountains late Thursday afternoon into Thursday night, while lower elevations and southeast Oregon remain mostly dry.

sections.name: Long Term
paragraphs: Friday, a closed low off the Pacific Northwest Coast amplifies along a southward trough axis capturing a pocket of tropical moisture. As a deep Alaskan Low strengthens, it captures the closed low, trough, and tropical moisture. As they move inland, the low heads northeastward and carries the moisture and colder air inside the trough up through the forecast area. The entire synoptic process takes place from Friday through early Monday, during which precipitation chances increase and temperatures/snow levels fall. The primary cold front passes early Sunday morning in the latest ensemble means, so the weather Friday and Saturday feature modest precip chances (10-40%, higher over terrain) and snow levels around 5-7 kft MSL. Temperatures during this period hover around to just above normal for this time of year. Halloween evening (Saturday), precipitation chances increase sharply to 40-70% as temperatures and snow levels begin to dip. Sunday morning snow levels drop to 4-6 kft MSL, and by Monday they drop further to 3.5-4.5 kft MSL. At least some snowfall is likely above 5 kft MSL, and at least some chance of snow exists down to 4 kft MSL even though precipitation chances begin to decrease Sunday night, limiting how much precipitation falls when snow levels are lowest. Dry conditions will prevail through the beginning of next week. Seasonable or below normal temperatures will continue through the long-term period.

BOU.name: Boulder / Denver
BOU.excerpt: There remains considerable uncertainty for the Monday and Tuesday period. Models indicate a piece of the broader western US trough will break off and become cutoff.

sections.name: Key Messages
paragraphs: - Another night of fog with visibility below 1/4 mile in the South Platte River Valley and the far eastern plains of Colorado.
- Mild and mostly dry through the work week.

- Unsettled weather potentially returning late in the weekend and early next week. There are many scenarios for how the weather will turn out but snow in the mountains is the most likely impact from this system. One possibility results in the lower elevations seeing their first snowfall of the season.

sections.name: Discussion
paragraphs: The fog and low clouds have mostly dissipated today except for Morgan County which has held onto some low clouds. With some low clouds lingering and a mountain wave cloud over Boulder, Larimer, Weld, and Morgan Counties, the high temperature forecast was lowered 2-3 F in those areas. Otherwise, there are no impacts expected today with dry conditions.

Overnight tonight, there will continue to be weak lee cyclogenesis over the eastern plains. The light easterly low level flow across the plains will push the low clouds and moisture currently over western Kansas and Nebraska back into Colorado. This will lead to another night of fog and low clouds. The worst visibility as low as 1/4 of a mile will be in the South Platte River Valley from Julesburg to Greeley. This fog will likely extended throughout the majority of southern Weld County but may not reach Adams, Boulder, or Larimer Counties. With that being said, the cities of Fort Collins and Longmont will have a 50% chance of fog tonight. This fog was added to the forecast generally from midnight to 9 AM Wednesday. There may need to be Dense Fog Advisories for the I-76 corridor.
Southwest flow aloft will be over Colorado Wednesday and Thursday with very dry air. This will keep conditions dry at the surface with generally pleasant conditions and seasonal temperatures.

On Friday, there will be a weak shortwave trough that will move over the panhandle of Texas. Our forecast area should be to the northwest of the precipitation and affects from this trough. However, some light precipitation could occur over Lincoln and Washington Counties as well as the central mountains. Otherwise, there will be seasonal temperatures and light winds.

Saturday and Sunday will have strong southwest flow aloft as a broad trough moves over the West Coast. There will be an initial very light wave of moisture that will move over the mountains of Colorado on Saturday that will produce light rain/snow. The plains will remain dry. On Sunday and into Sunday night, mid to upper level moisture with origins from the tropical Pacific will move from southern California to Colorado. This will bring another shot of rain/snow to the mountains of our forecast area. Since this moisture has tropical origins, snow levels will be high, likely above 9,500 feet or even above 10,000 feet. The other thing to note about the Sunday and Sunday night system is that in southwest flow aloft, the mountains of our forecast area usually under perform because the mountains of southwest Colorado usually receive the bulk of the moisture.

There remains considerable uncertainty for the Monday and Tuesday period. Models indicate a piece of the broader western US trough will break off and become cutoff. This cutoff trough will generally move from the Idaho/Montana region towards Colorado and then to the Central Plains. There are many scenarios that could play out with this system. It could track east of our forecast area bringing light snow to the northern mountains and mostly dry conditions to the plains. It could track well west of our forecast area, perhaps in Utah, and provide some mountain snowfall and light precipitation across the plains. Another possibility is that it tracks just to the west of our forecast area and creates strong easterly flow in the low levels and a more significant precipitation event for our area. Given that the trough is breaking off of a larger trough and becoming cutoff, the predictability is quite low and none of the scenarios are favored at the moment. Expect forecast models to vary greatly from run to run over the next few days. Nonetheless, it is a system worth watching.

CYS.name: Cheyenne
CYS.excerpt: In lieu of that, we can discuss some possible scenarios. Approximately 45% of LREF members are clustered into a scenario showing a more progressive storm system.

sections.name: Key Messages
paragraphs: - Drier, warmer, and breezy to windy conditions are expected to continue through Wednesday. Another round of morning fog is possible over portions of the High Plains Wednesday AM.
- Chances for a few showers return Friday into Saturday (Halloween) with temperatures remaining mild.
- A pattern change to colder, wetter, and windier conditions is favored Sunday into Tuesday, but the details remain highly uncertain at this time.

sections.name: Short Term
paragraphs: It's still a bit breezy this afternoon as the 700mb jet slowly begins to calm down. While high winds aren't expected this afternoon wind gusts between 45 and 55 mph can still be anticipated on I-80 between Rawlins and Laramie as well as I-25 in between Casper and Douglas. As the system continues to lift back into the Canadian Providences we will continue to see the 700mb jet weaken and the upper level ridge begin to take back over. Other than some high level clouds moving through the area not much should be expected in the short term forecast. Another weak shortwave is expected to be passing through the Intermountain west tonight. We will see some increased cloud cover and stable temperatures overnight around 40 to 45 degrees. But otherwise any precip chances look to be contained in the Northwestern portion of Wyoming and possibly Central Wyoming. Under this ridge 700mb temperatures are going to be around 6C which means high temperatures will be around 60 to 65 for locations east of the I-25 corridor and between 50 and 55 for the higher elevations west of the I-25 corridor.

sections.name: Long Term
paragraphs: On Friday, we will once again see a broad ridge in place over the Central CONUS. This iteration of this familiar weather pattern will be less amplified, not supporting warmth as significant as what we had earlier this month. With troughing inching into the west coast, southwest flow aloft will continue to prevail. Models are in fairly good agreement showing low-level south to southeast winds advecting in improved low-level moisture to the High Plains Friday while moisture aloft improves with another influx of tropical moisture. By the end of the day Friday, NAEFS mean precipitable water exceeds the 90th percentile of climatology for much of the area. As has been our problem frequently as of late, we will not have much forcing for ascent, despite the abundant moisture. This begins to change Friday night as two disturbances are pulled out of the southwest. The first will be associated with the remnant moisture of Tropical Storm Vance, the latest in the parade of eastern Pacific tropical systems pushed into the southwest CONUS. This remnant vort-max will track further east than its predecessors, moving mostly over the Plains. There is a possibility (about 30% chance) for some showers Friday night into Saturday, mainly in the Nebraska panhandle. Another more disorganized vort-max tracking further west will bring potential for afternoon and evening showers and high elevation snow showers mainly to the mountains and adjacent zones on Saturday (Halloween). Other than the potential for a few light showers, expect generally good trick-or-treat conditions with highs in the mid 50s to mid 60s and overnight lows dropping only into the upper 30s to mid 40s. Winds look fairly light as well.

Forecast confidence decreases considerably as we head into the Sunday through Tuesday time period. While there is still potential for widespread precipitation, the ensemble spread is enormous as a very complex weather pattern sets up over the Western CONUS. First, a powerful disturbance will race into the southwest, riding on a very strong sub-tropical jet stream. Meanwhile, a northern branch trough will dive into the northwest and progress eastward simultaneously. The northern upper level low may also close off from the polar jet itself, adding to the uncertainty. With so many moving parts on the board, it is difficult to have much forecast confidence in how this will play out.

In lieu of that, we can discuss some possible scenarios. Approximately 45% of LREF members are clustered into a scenario showing a more progressive storm system. This is further split between about half of this camp showing a storm that remains progressive, and half showing a storm that eventually closes off and strengthens, but this occurs too far east to deliver much precipitation to our area. In this scenario, most of the area could expect light precipitation amounts, generally 0.25" or less. The remaining 55% of ensemble members have a deeper, stronger system with better forcing for lift, and thus improving chances for precipitation. About 30% of the full ensemble suite (a subset of the 55%) have a moderate precipitation event, where the system is strong and deep, but still progressive. The final 25% (again a subset of the 55%) depict a slow, strong upper level low closing off before reaching our area, which would lead to widespread heavy precipitation for much of the area, but especially over the High Plains. The ECMWF Extreme Forecast Index provides some additional context. EFI values for QPF on Monday are only around 0.5 to 0.7, suggesting low confidence in a significant event. However, the shift of tails values exceed 2.0 over much of the High Plains, which tells us that a small subset of ensemble members depict an extreme event. Thus, the main takeaway at this time should be that at least some light precipitation is narrowly favored (60% chance) over much of the area Sunday PM into Tuesday AM, and there is potential for significant rain and/or snow, but the probability of this scenario is fairly low (25% chance) at this time. Nonetheless, this is high enough to discuss and continue to monitor closely in the coming days. Most model guidance shows limited cold air with this system once again, and the wettest ensemble members also tend to be the warmest (as these close the low off faster). This will make snow levels an issue once again. Regardless of the precipitation outcome, expect cooler temperatures by Monday with blustery conditions. There is potential for high winds as well, but we'll wait to get a better idea of the storm's evolution before diving into those details.

GJT.name: Grand Junction
GJT.excerpt: As flow turns southwesterly ahead of a PacNW low, moisture begins its return to the region. The first signs of this pattern shift are expected on Friday as isolated storms will begin to pop up, though at this point QPF should be on the minimal side.

sections.name: Key Messages
paragraphs: - Monday through Thursday is expected to be mostly dry with another impactful system possible by the weekend.
- Model guidance reflects some uncertainty in storm tracks, leading to inconsistencies in moisture and river volume forecasts.

sections.name: Discussion
paragraphs: Near-zonal flow is established across the Intermountain West today, maintaining relatively dry conditions for our CWA. This keeps precipitation chances near-zero for most locations with little more than scattered cloud cover expected. We're sitting near-normal in terms of high temperatures as well, leaving valleys in the 50's to low-60's, and mountain locations in the 40's to low-50's. Though we continue to dry out steadily the next few days, some valley locations may still experience fog around sunrise which may impact morning commutes.
NEXT ROUND OF PRECIPITATION THIS WEEKEND:

As flow turns southwesterly ahead of a PacNW low, moisture begins its return to the region. The first signs of this pattern shift are expected on Friday as isolated storms will begin to pop up, though at this point QPF should be on the minimal side. By Sunday though, moisture will be hitting its peak in our CWA. As guidance stands there is little confidence in the exact trajectory of the broad moisture plume. If we are to lean one way or another, more evidence is suggesting that the strongest portion of the plume will pass to our south, though even in this scenario, southwestern Colorado is in line for yet another wet stretch with PWAT's up to 300% of normal. Adding to the complexity of this event is the progression of the upper-level pattern. As the PacNW low propagates eastwards towards the northern Rockies, a second low develops at the base of the trough, swinging through the southwestern portion of the county before eventually rejoining the parent trough early in the work week. The movement of both lows would likely have significant impacts on the nature of this storm system as temperatures will plummet to around 10 degrees below normal with their passage. This could be enough to drop snow level 1-2 kft. The complex pattern continues to lead to weak confidence in the timing and location of any eventual snowfall though, and as such we cannot yet speculate on how impacts will manifest from said snowfall. What we can say now though is that any notable amount of precipitation over southwestern Colorado locations recovering from last week's rainfall will have the potential to exacerbate flooding concerns. We are keeping a very close eye on this next round of precipitation as a result, and over the coming days as more details come into view we will begin to better gauge the risks Sunday into Monday morning. As such, stay tuned for additional information throughout this week.

PUB.name: Pueblo
PUB.excerpt: Overall, we should see storm system which brings beneficial snow pack to the the mountains Sunday-TUesday. Of interest, per USGS, Lake Powell has risen 14 feet since mid September.

sections.name: Key Messages
paragraphs: - An area of subtropical moisture may affect far SE CO Friday; Showers possible in the mtns.
- More impactful storm to affect the region late Saturday into late Tuesday.

sections.name: Short Term
paragraphs: Weather will continue to be quiet from the rest os today into early Friday. Anticipate mild temps in the 60s and 70s plains and 50s larger valleys. Warmest day will be tomorrow.

sections.name: Long Term
paragraphs: On Friday, an area of subtropical moisture is forecast to move north- northeast from old Mexico and move towards far southeast Colorado. This area of moisture, if it verifies, could bring a period or precip to far southeast Colorado on Friday, However, I have seen situations similar to this one in the past, with the moisture moving too far east and moving into KS. For now my confidence is not high on this forecast verifying.
In the meantime, moisture will increase over the higher terrain, and we will likely see some isolated to scattered showers in the mountains on Friday.
For Saturday, weak mid level ridging moves over the region. Any showers which develop this day will be isolated, and mainly confined to the higher terrain.

The weather ramps up Sunday and is fcst to last into Tuesday. A Sharp mid level trough is fcst to drop southeast from the Pacific northwest. As this trough move through, another band of subtropical moisture coming off the California coast moves across the region. At this time this looks to be a mountain storm. Temps will be warm initially, but will cool off quite a bit as the mid level trough moves towards the region. Overall, we would see some rain at higher elevations initially, but believe the brunt of the precip in the mtns will be snow. This is shown in the NBM 1D forecast statistical products for the higher elevation points to our west.

With that said, if the storm does wrap up considerably as it moves into KS, we could get some wrap-around moisture over the plains, especially during the Monday/Tuesday time frame. If the system drops a bit farther south and east as hinted by the latest 12Z EC, then the plains may see a more favorable upslope pattern develop.

How this system impacts us will be very dependent on the track and intensification of the trough. Usually storms dropping southeast and intensifying as they do, can bring impactful weather to the region.
Overall, we should see storm system which brings beneficial snow pack to the the mountains Sunday-TUesday. Of interest, per USGS, Lake Powell has risen 14 feet since mid September.

SLC.name: Salt Lake City
SLC.excerpt: Behind the exiting system, a ridge is expected to develop off the Pacific coast, likely bringing an at least temporary end to the active pattern as of late.

sections.name: Key Messages
paragraphs: - Generally dry and seasonable conditions will persist through Thursday, with a weak grazing system tonight into Wednesday morning bringing a low chance of precipitation near the Utah/Idaho border.

- Moisture will increase over the area beginning Friday, bringing an increasing threat of flash flooding. The area will see a more substantial increase in moisture and instability and thus the potential for flooding Sunday into Monday as a strong Pacific storm crosses the area.
- Much cooler temperatures will accompany the system for early next week, allowing snow levels to potentially drop as low as 7500 feet by Monday morning.

sections.name: Discussion
paragraphs: Seeing a roughly zonal flow across Utah and southwest Wyoming this morning between an exit weak storm system and another Pacific Northwest storm system that will graze northern portions of the area tonight into Wednesday morning. Currently seeing mostly clear skies with some mid-level clouds near the Utah/Idaho border. Maxes today should run close to seasonal normals across the vast majority of the area.

With the passage of the next grazing system and associated front overnight, impacts should be similar to the one that just moved through. That is, the front will act to curb any warming trend and will bring a few showers near the Utah/Idaho border. Seasonable temperatures will continue through Thursday, with southerly flow gradually increasing.

Two storm system are expected to approach the Pacific coast Thursday, with the weaker southern one merging with the Pacific Northwest one by Friday. The southerly flow is expected to tap into some deeper moisture during the day Friday, with ejecting shortwaves out ahead of the main system providing additional instability. This will bring scattered showers and thunderstorms focused over southern Utah, bringing the potential for isolated flash flooding. Guidance overall is trending downward with coverage of precipitation with this part of the event, though at least some potential remains. In between systems, there should be a relative lull in convection on Saturday.

For Sunday, the previously mentioned Pacific Northwest storm system is expected to merge with a decaying tropical system before tracking across the area Sunday into Monday. The amount of moisture anticipated to accompany the system should be near records for this time of year, with the potent system and its strong associated cold front providing additional lift. This should bring widespread coverage of precipitation across utah and southwest Wyoming during the day Sunday, and given how saturated soils already are across southern Utah from the previous tropical events as of late, additional heavy rain has the potential to be that much more impactful. It should be noted, however, that this system is expected to be more progressive in nature than previous events and the associated precipitation a bit more steady in nature, providing a little bit in the way of limiting factors.

Given its Pacific Northwest origin, this system will also bring much colder air into the region, resulting in temperatures averaging 10-15F below seasonal normals to start the upcoming week. This influx of cold air will steadily lower snow levels through Monday morning, with a high chance of those snow levels moving into the 7000 to 8000 ft range.
Behind the exiting system, a ridge is expected to develop off the Pacific coast, likely bringing an at least temporary end to the active pattern as of late.

2755.travel_advice: Watch for signs of unstable snow such as recent avalanches, cracking in the snow, and audible collapsing. Avoid traveling on or under similar slopes.

product.author: Jason Konigsberg
bottom_line: Heavy rain on Wednesday and Thursday triggered small wet avalanches in the west-Central and Southern Mountains, but this concern is waning as temperatures drop. The most likely place to trigger an avalanche is at the highest elevations (above about 12,500 feet) in the Southern and west-Central Mountains on west, north, and east-facing slopes where new snow has been accumulating and a layer of mid-October snow persists. The Northern Mountains remain mostly bare.

This weekend, a new storm will deliver 4 to 8 inches of snow to the San Juan and Sangre de Cristo Mountains, creating fresh avalanche concerns on upper-elevation, wind-drifted slopes facing west, north, and east. Early-season travelers, including hunters and hikers, should use caution on steep terrain because even shallow snow on grassy slopes, rock slabs, or old snowfields can slide.

We will provide updates as needed until our daily forecasts resume on November 1, 2026. Please continue submitting your field observations, and check our website for real-time weather station data and model forecasts.

product.author: Kevin Studley
hazard_discussion: Avalanche Forecasting Operations Have Come to a Close for the 2026-26 Season
Have a safe spring in the mountains. Continue to remain vigilant and flexible while traveling in the mountains this spring.
OBSERVATIONS

Observations are still greatly appreciated. Spring-time observations are extremely helpful as forecast operations have come to a close. If you're out in the mountains, submit an observation to let the rest of the public know what's going on out there. Even a simple weather observation can be very useful.
• View recent observations HERE
• Submit an observation HERE
• Recent photos and videos HERE
Snow and Avalanche Information
• Dry Slab avalanche problems such as storm slab and wind slab avalanches are most likely during and immediately following a storm.

• Wet Loose avalanches are expected during warmups and (even brief) clear, sunny weather events, and rain events. Watch for pinwheels and rollerballs as an indicator the snow is becoming damp. If you're sinking into soft, mushy snow, it's time to turn around or find a different aspect.

• Wet Slab avalanches become likely during rain events and with multiple nights above freezing. Wet slabs occur when melt water pools and lubricates crusts or older persistent weak layers. Wet slab avalanches are notoriously difficult to predict.
• Cornices are large and often become unstable during prolonged warmups. Give yourself plenty of space above and below them. They tend to begin shedding during warming and/or rain events.
• Dry Loose Snow avalanches are expected during and immediately after a storm, particularly on shaded, north-facing slopes.

• Glide avalanches typically fail in similar spots year after year after an abundance of meltwater has saturated the ground or lower snowpack. Glide avalanches can occur in steep terrain, on smooth grassy slopes or on large slabs of rock. Look for glide cracks opening up during spring.
WEATHER
• Click HERE to view our Weather Station Map page with updated webcams
• Click HERE to view our Weather Tools page
• Spring weather patterns are often erratic and snow conditions can change quickly during spring weather. Be attentive to these changes and remain flexible with your travel plans.
• Rain on snow events can create dangerous avalanche conditions in a short period of time.
• Spring time means a higher sun angle, with direct solar radiation on the snowpack. Even a brief dose of sunshine can quickly alter the snow surface.

• Overcast skies and snow showers can open up to full sunshine in a matter of minutes. Convective snow showers can be spotty and difficult to forecast. Temperatures can vary depending on elevation and unexpected cloud cover can significantly alter a weather forecast.
OTHER CONSIDERATIONS
• Travel
• As people push into steeper, more consequential terrain, remember to maintain safe travel protocols and not let your guard down just because it's sunny and warm.
• During melt-freeze cycles, pay attention to "slide-for-life" circumstances, particularly during morning travel.
• Be mindful of terrain selection and timing. Identify terrain traps and be prepared to avoid/manage them.
• Spring Mindset

• Springtime is when mountain travelers push for bigger objectives. We have greater confidence in the stability of the snowpack and the high sun angle makes us feel ready to charge. As we start stepping out into bigger terrain in the mountains, be mindful of consequences (ask yourself, "If this slides, what will happen?"). Choose your terrain appropriately and manage new/surface snow problems accordingly. Be aware that dynamic weather can have quick impacts on the snow surface. A common theme I've noticed over the last 15 years playing in steep, snowy mountains is that experienced, seasoned people often get caught in small avalanches in big terrain during the spring. We have a tendency to underestimate "manageable" new snow problems like wind slab and loose snow. Pay attention to changing weather and know that small shifts in spring weather can have dramatic impacts on the upper snowpack.
